query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled secondary heat treatment can be applied to induce the in situ formation of coherent nanoprecipitates along the internal lamellar boundaries of the eutectic HEA, which will reduce dislocation pile-ups and local stress concentrations, thereby overcoming brittle behavior and limited tensile ductility while retaining or even enhancing strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies that suffers from dislocation pile-up at internal boundaries leading to stress concentrations, microcracking, and brittle failure at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Implement a secondary heat treatment step designed to promote the formation of coherent, nanoscale precipitates specifically at the lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing under standard ambient conditions; heat treatment parameters (temperature and duration) must be optimized to yield coherent precipitates without overgrowth. Microstructural evaluations (e.g., TEM) would be carried out post-treatment.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nano-precipitates located along the internal lamellar interfaces that modify the boundary characteristics.
generation.mechanism: The coherent nanoprecipitates act as controlled dislocation transmission sites. They help to alleviate local stress concentration by reducing dislocation pile-up at the interfaces and facilitate more uniform plastic deformation; at the same time, they contribute to precipitation strengthening, thus either retaining or enhancing the overall tensile strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the treated material should show increased tensile ductility (i.e., greater elongation to failure) at room temperature while maintaining or slightly improving yield and ultimate tensile strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated eutectic HEA with dual-phase lamellar colonies that shows limited room-temperature ductility and premature failure due to dislocation pile-ups and microcracking.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated under room-temperature tensile loading and will depend on precise control of the heat treatment parameters. Deviations may lead to over-precipitation or formation of incoherent secondary phases and could compromise performance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the ductility improvement and strength retention/enhancement is uncertain and requires careful optimization of the processing conditions. There is a risk that if the heat-treatment parameters are not properly controlled, incoherent phases or over-precipitation might occur, which could worsen the mechanical response.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one set to receive the optimized secondary heat treatment to induce coherent nanoprecipitation, and a control set kept as-cast. Perform room-temperature tensile tests and detailed TEM analyses to assess microstructural changes, particularly at the lamellar boundaries.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
TEM characterization of internal boundaries for evidence of coherent nanoprecipitates and reduced dislocation pile-up
Fractographic analysis to quantify microcrack density and distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in tensile ductility and/or if TEM reveals that the nanoprecipitates are incoherent or fail to mitigate dislocation pile-ups (with persistent local stress concentrations and microcracking similar to the untreated condition), the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.
